analysis.one_liner: Taxes 50% of big oil's windfall profits and rebates the money to taxpayers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and died there when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have put a 50% excise tax on the excess profits of large crude oil companies — measured as the amount that oil prices rose above their 2015-2019 average — and paid all of the money back to individual taxpayers as quarterly gasoline price rebates. Companies extracting or importing more than 300,000 barrels a day would pay; smaller producers would not. Rebates would phase out for higher incomes. The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, especially lower- and middle-income households, who would receive quarterly rebates out of the windfall tax collected. The rebate phases out above $75,000 of income for single filers and $150,000 for joint filers, so the money concentrates toward lower incomes [S3]. Joint filers would receive 150% of the individual rebate amount [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 50% excise tax on each barrel of crude oil extracted or imported by large companies, at a rate equal to 50% of the amount by which the quarterly average Brent crude price exceeds its 2015-2019 average price.
Applies only to taxpayers who extracted and imported more than 300,000 barrels of crude oil per day in 2019 or in the current quarter, so the tax falls on the largest oil companies.
Creates a 'Protect Consumers from Gas Hikes Fund' and requires all tax collected to be rebated to individual taxpayers, with payments made quarterly within 90 days of the end of each quarter.

Phases the rebate out for higher incomes — reduced by 5% of income above $75,000 for single filers, $112,500 for heads of household, and $150,000 for joint filers — and makes the credit refundable so households with little or no income tax liability still receive it.

analysis.who_pays: Large crude oil producers and refiners — companies extracting or importing more than 300,000 barrels a day — would pay the 50% excise tax on barrels sold at prices above the pre-2020 benchmark. Economists warn some of the tax could be passed through to consumers at the pump and that taxing windfall profits may discourage future investment in oil production.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big crude oil producers and refiners

drawbacks.text: The tax is not capped at recent profits — it applies whenever quarterly Brent prices exceed their 2015-2019 average, so it would keep collecting in ordinary price environments, not only true windfalls, and the 2015-2019 benchmark period included unusually low prices.

A standard objection to windfall profits taxes is that they reduce the expected return on future drilling and production, which can discourage the investment that keeps oil supply — and eventually prices — down; the rebate could also blunt consumers' incentive to cut gasoline use.
The rebate amount is unpredictable: it depends on whatever revenue the tax happens to raise in the prior quarter, so households would not know in advance how large their payments would be.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: During the 2022 gasoline price spike, the bill offered a direct trade: take a portion of the largest oil companies' abnormal profits and hand it back to consumers. The design has real weaknesses — the benchmark can collect tax in non-windfall times, the tax may dampen future supply investment, and rebate sizes would be unpredictable — but the bill's core purpose, redirecting windfall gains from a concentrated industry to lower- and middle-income households, is clear. The stronger design objections do not change the basic fact of who would have gained and who would have paid.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse and 11 other senators introduced the Big Oil Windfall Profits Tax Act on March 10, 2022.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action was ever recorded: the bill received no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote.
The bill attracted 17 cosponsors — 16 of the 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of the 2 independents — and no Republican cosponsors.

The bill would have imposed a 50% excise tax on crude oil barrels priced above their 2015-2019 average, paid by companies extracting or importing more than 300,000 barrels per day, and rebated all proceeds to individual taxpayers through a quarterly credit.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large crude oil companies are better off because the bill died: none of them paid the 50% windfall tax, and no consumer rebates were ever issued.

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its promotion.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Chaired the Finance Committee, which never brought the bill to a markup or vote during the 117th Congress.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors were Democrats or independents and no Republican signed on; no vote ever occurred, so the full Senate never took a position.

industries.industry: Large crude oil producers and refiners
industries.note: The bill would have taken 50% of their barrels' value above a pre-2020 price benchmark, applying only to companies moving more than 300,000 barrels a day. In this bill their financial interest ran directly against the consumers who would have received the rebates.
The 300,000-barrel daily threshold would have exempted them from the windfall tax entirely, giving them a cost advantage over the largest companies.
